result.findings:
Based on the search results, a **Strait of Hormuz blockade has already occurred as of March 2026**, moving beyond hypothetical scenarios into an active crisis. The blockade followed US-Israeli military attacks against Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.[1][6]

## Current Blockade Status

On March 2, 2026, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) declared that any vessel attempting to pass through the strait would be attacked.[6] Ship-tracking data confirms Iran has been largely successful in shutting down traffic: the strait averaged more than 153 vessel transits daily before the conflict, but since March 1, only 78 vessels have passed through in total, averaging just 13 per day.[6] This blockade removes approximately **20 million barrels of oil per day from global markets**, representing 20% of the world's petroleum liquids and 20% of global LNG trade.[1]

## Pre-2026 Expert Analysis on Probability

Prior expert assessments suggested Iran would only attempt a blockade under existential threat. During the June 2025 Israel-Iran conflict, when the US targeted three Iranian nuclear facilities on June 22, Iran chose not to close the strait, instead conducting a calibrated attack on a US military base in Qatar with advance warning to Qatar and the US.[8] This indicated Iran viewed other options as preferable escalation measures.

However, experts acknowledged Iran possessed the capability to execute a blockade through multiple methods: approximately 5,000-6,000 naval mines deployable via roughly 25 submarines (including three Russian Kilo-class and 23 domestically-produced Ghadir-class mini-submarines), and a coastal defense network with anti-ship missiles including Khalij-e Fars ballistic missiles (300-kilometer range) and C-802 Noor cruise missiles (120-kilometer range).[7]

## Economic Impact Projections

Expert forecasts for oil prices in a blockade scenario varied substantially: Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister warned prices could reach $200-300 per barrel, JPMorgan analysts projected $130 per barrel, while CME Group estimated a more modest $13.50 per barrel increase.[3] The blockade also threatens a 20% reduction in global LNG supplies.[1] China faces particular vulnerability, as the strait transports approximately 50% of its oil imports, jeopardizing industrial output and power grids.[1] Japan imports 1.6 million barrels daily through the strait, and South Korea channels 68% of its crude imports (1.7 million barrels daily) through Hormuz.[2]
